# Server Paging in Phoenix

Dec 06, 2020, Kadir Ozdemir v0, Initial draft

Phoenix performs two main operations on the server side: aggregation and filtering. However, currently there is no internal Phoenix paging capability, and thus server side operations can take long enough to lead to HBase client timeouts. Because of these timeouts, the synchronous operations (the operations initiated by the JDBC interface) cannot be reliably used for the queries that potentially scan a large number of cells on the server side. To circumvent this problem, the long running operations are executed asynchronously using MapReduce where mappers set the HBase RPC timeouts to very large values. This results in long running operations. These long running operations can lead to overall HBase cluster availability issues by holding resources such as threads, RPC handlers, region locks, etc. This design document introduces paging capabilities in Phoenix region scanners and filters ([PHOENIX-5998](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/PHOENIX-5998), [PHOENIX-6207](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/PHOENIX-6207), and [PHOENIX-6211](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/PHOENIX-6211)) to allow these operations to be submitted synchronously using the JDBC interface without increasing timeout values.  

# Requirements

1. Phoenix (main or sub) queries issued via the JDBC interface should not cause HBase RPC timeouts. The SQL statements covered by this requirement include SELECT, DELETE, and UPSERT SELECT statements.  
2. The above SQL statements should not lead to cluster availability and responsiveness issues.  
3. The above requirements should be satisfied without noticeable performance panalties. 

# Background

Conceptually, the result of a query at the JDBC interface or the result of a table scan at the HBase client or server interface is a set. The elements of this set are accessed using an iterator. This iterator interface is called ResultSet in the JDBC API where a ResultSet is generated from a (query) statement. The entries iterated over are implicit rows which are the result of the execution of the query statement.   

Internally, Phoenix translated the query in a JDBC statement into a query plan (called QueryPlan) which generates an iterator called ResultIterator. The entries of this iterator are called Tuple. A tuple is an internal representation of a table row.  

Table is the interface to represent a table in the HBase client API. The iterator generated by the table object is called ResultScanner. The entries this iterator returns are the rows of the table and they are called Result. Result is essentially a map of cells which are indexed by their family name and qualifier.

At an HBase region server, a table region (called Region) returns an iterator called RegionScanner to scan over the rows of a table region. In each iteration a list of cells is returned.

# Problem Statement

The way we modelled the end-to-end read path in the previous section allows us to reduce the timeout issue tackled in this design document to not having a time limit on the loops within Phoenix and HBase region scanners. 

The reason for the loop within a Phoenix region scanner can take a long time is simply that the number of rows to be processed for an aggregation operation within a single RPC can be too large.  For example, counting the number of rows in a table region within a single RPC can take long enough to cause HBase client RPC timeout.  
   
A table region can have a large number of cells and the filter set on the HBase region scanner can be very selective. This means that to return even a single row, the region scanner may have to scan a large number of cells and this can take a long time. Even when the filter is not very selective, returning a single row can take a long time due large number delete type cells.     

# High-Level Design

In order to put a time limit on the amount of work done with an RPC, this design introduces the paging capability in Phoenix region scanners and filters. A page is a set of rows to be scanned and processed at each invocation of the next operation on a region scanner.  The number of rows in a page is determined by a time limit. In order words, the page size is defined by time.  

When a next operation returns, it returns a result which is a set of cells. This means when a page of work is done, a Phoenix region scanner needs to return a result. However, completing a page of work does not mean that the region scanner is ready to return a meaningful result. For example, grouping or sorting rows based on the values of a column may require many pages but can only return a meaningful result after all pages are done. This means the Phoenix region scanner needs to return a dummy result to the Phoenix client that would simply skip this dummy result and ask for another result by issuing another next operation. Thus, this design introduces the concept of a dummy result.  A dummy result consists of one cell with null family name, qualifier, and value.

What has been described so far is a sufficient solution for introducing a paging capability in a Phoenix region scanner. This solution requires changing the region scanner loop to put a time limit on the loop and return a dummy result when needed. Since this paging capability is for Phoenix, we would like to introduce a paging capability for HBase region scanner without changing the HBase code. We can achieve this by using a custom HBase filter.

The HBase client API provides a public class called Scan to specify which rows of a table to be scanned. In addition to the properties of Scan such as startRow and stopRow,  timeRange, etc, we can set a filter on the scan object to have further filtering of rows. HBase comes with a wide range of filters and also allows custom filters. Phoenix has its own (HBase custom) filters and use them in combination with HBase filters as filters can be combined using the logical operators (i.e., “and” and “or”) within the class FilterList. In addition, we wrap a filter inside another filter too.

In this design, we introduce a custom filter called PagedFilter to provide paging. This filter wraps the already set filter on the scan, if any. The sole purpose of this filter is to check if an HBase region scanner has spent too much time on scanning rows. If so, this custom filter terminates the scan. 

In addition to the custom filter, the design introduced a wrapper region scanner called PagedRegionScanner which wraps the HBase region scanner and works together with PagedFilter to detect if the HBase scanner is stopped by PagedFilter and if so, it closes the scanner and start a new HBase region scanner from the last row the previous scanner visited. When this happens, PagedRegionScanner returns a dummy result to the Phoenix region scanner which in turn returns this dummy result to the Phoenix client.  The ResultIterator object in the Phoenix client seeing this dummy result ignores it and issues the next operation. The end-to-end data path architecture is updated with the new design as shown below.

# Detailed Design

## Client

The JDBC ResultSet interface is implemented by PhoenixResultSet class. This class has a ResultIterator object. ResultIterator is an interface. The classes of the ResultIterator object referred by PhoenixResultSet are the top level ResultIterator classes. The examples of classes are ConcatResultIterator, MergeSortTopNResultIterator and RoundRobinResultIterator. 

The lowest level ResultIterator is ScanningResultIterator which gets a ResultScanner object for an HBase table. ScanningResultIterator is also responsible for updating scan metrics.  Another ResultIterator class called TableResultIterator which wraps ScanningResultIterator is called TableResultIterator. 

Based on the type of the query, a Phoenix client scans table regions of a table in parallel or serially. Typically, it allocates a separate TableResultIterator object for each table region it will scan. These objects are grouped under a ResultIterators object. ParallelIterator and SerialIterator implement the ResultIterators interface. A ResultIterators object is then referred to by a top level ResultIterator object. This is illustrated in the following diagram.

This design adds the logic to ScanningResultIterator skip the dummy Result objects from a ResultScanner object and call the next() operation again on the ResultScanner object for each dummy result. As explained before, this dummy result objects are generated by the paging capability implemented by the Phoenix server side code, i.e., Phoenix region scanners. 

A new scan attribute is defined called \_ServerPageSizeMs to set the page size for the server operation within a single RPC. This page size is by default set to 60% of the HBase RPC timeout value configured on the client side. This page size is used for the loops within Phoenix region scanner while the page size for HBase region scanner is set to half of this value. This is to make sure that the total operation time within a single RPC would not exceed the timeout value. 

We also add a new configuration parameter called phoenix.server.page.size.ms to overwrite the default value. We should not need to configure this parameter. This parameter is also used for testing purposes as explained later.

## Server

Phoenix has a stack of RegionScanner and ResultIterator objects on the server side. These   
objects are allocated by the Phoenix coprocs which are PhoenixTTLRegionObserver, GlobalIndexChecker, ScanRegionObserver, GroupAggregateRegionObserver and UngroupedAggregateRegionObserver. We do not really need to know exactly what each object does but we need to know if the object has a loop of next() operations, and if so, we need to make sure that each loop is time bound and checks if a dummy result is returned from the lower layer. When the loop spends the allowed time (i.e., the page size in ms) then it has to terminate and returns a dummy result. Also, when a dummy result is received from the lower layer, the loop has to terminate and pass the dummy result to the next layer up. The objects with the next() loop are labelled with a loop sign in the diagram below.

## PagedFilter

PageFilter fields are shown in the following UML diagram.

![][image1]

PageFilter behaves as a pass-through object in states STARTED and TIME\_TO\_STOP by forwarding filter method calls to its delegate if the delegate exists. At state TIME\_TO\_STOP, it sets the current row key to rowKeyAtStop in Filter\#filterRowKey(). 

## PagedRegionScanner

PagedRegionScanner fields are shown in the UML diagram below. PagedRegionScanner is mostly a pass-through object. It checks if the next() operation on the delegate region scanner which is implemented by HBase returns false which means either no more rows left (i.e., the scan on the table region is ended) or PageFilter stopped the scanned. Then PagedRegionScanner checks the state on the PagedFilter object.  If the state is STOPPED, then PagedRegionScanner returns a dummy result, then it closes the delegate scanner and starts it from PagedFilter\#rowKeyAtStop (inclusive). 

PagedRegionScanner resets the startTime on its PagedFilter after every non dummy result returned by the HBase region scanner if the PageFilter is in the STARTED state. This means the paging is applicable to the back-to-back filtered rows. If there is not a large number of back-to-back filtered rows then paging would not happen in HBase region scanners.   
![][image2]

# Alternative Approaches

In the Phoenix master branch, the HBase client exchanges heartbeat messages with the HBase region server to prevent timeouts and ResultScanner can return a special Result (similar to the dummy result introduced in this design) called cursor if this is enabled using Scan\#setNeedCursorResult(). It is not clear how this cursor functionality can be used within a coproc but if it can be used then this would eliminate the need for PagedFilter. Since this cursor functionality is not available in the Phoenix 4.x branch, this alternative approach has not been pursued further.

Another approach would be to use HBase ScannerContext instead of using PagedFilter to put a time limit on the HBase RegionScanner next operation execution time. ScannerContext is for tracking more than just time but also size and batch. It has a richer and more complex interface than PagedFilter has. However, it does not seem to have any advantage over PagedFilter if it is used for tracking time. BaseRegionScanner and DelegateRegionScanner classes in Phoenix return IOException if ScannerContext is used at this moment.  The reason for throwing this exception is not clear. The exception message is “NextRaw with scannerContext should not be called in Phoenix environment”.   

# Testing Strategy

The paging capability impacts any features enabled on the read path and there are a large number of ITs for them. We need all these tests exercised on the paging code. To do that we set the page sizes for region scanners and filter to 0ms. This results in at most one row pages. In other words, with this page size, every test exercises paging code.

# Performance Impact

The checks for dummy results that are introduced to the read path is very light in computation and should not cause any noticeable performance impact. When paging happens (i.e., the next() loop is terminated due to the page size) in a Phoenix region scanner, the dummy result is returned. Since the page size is set to 60% of the HBase RPC timeout value, the number of extra RPCs due to paging will be very minimal and should not cause any permanence impact either. Paging in a Phoenix filter will only happen if no row is selected within 30% of the HBase RPC timeout value, this will be a rare event and no performance impact is expected because of these events. During ITs, paging happens after every scanned row in Phoenix region scanners and after every row that is filtered. Even with this extreme paging, no performance impact on ITs has been observed.
